claim: Before primary motor cortex (M1) develops its motor functions, it functions like a somatosensory area.
source: Before primary motor cortex (M1) develops its motor functions, it functions like a somatosensory area.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract summarizing the main finding of the study.

claim: At P8-10, M1 neurons respond overwhelmingly to feedback from sleep-related twitches of the forelimb.
source: At P8-10, M1 neurons respond overwhelmingly to feedback from sleep-related twitches of the forelimb, but the same neurons do not respond to wake-related movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recordings from M1 neurons at P8-10 showing responses to twitches.

claim: At P8-10, M1 neurons do not respond to wake-related movements.
source: At P8-10, M1 neurons respond overwhelmingly to feedback from sleep-related twitches of the forelimb, but the same neurons do not respond to wake-related movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recordings showing lack of M1 responses to wake movements at P8-10.

claim: By P12, M1 neurons suddenly respond to wake movements.
source: By P12, M1 neurons suddenly respond to wake movements, a transition that results from opening the sensory gate in the external cuneate nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recordings at P12 showing M1 responses to wake movements.

claim: The transition to wake movement responsiveness at P12 results from opening the sensory gate in the external cuneate nucleus.
source: By P12, M1 neurons suddenly respond to wake movements, a transition that results from opening the sensory gate in the external cuneate nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by ECN recordings showing changes in sensory gating between P9 and P12.

claim: At P12, fewer M1 neurons respond to individual twitches.
source: Also at P12, fewer M1 neurons respond to individual twitches, but the full complement of twitch-related feedback observed at P8 is unmasked through local disinhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by recordings showing decreased twitch responsiveness at P12.

claim: The full complement of twitch-related feedback observed at P8 is unmasked through local disinhibition at P12.
source: Also at P12, fewer M1 neurons respond to individual twitches, but the full complement of twitch-related feedback observed at P8 is unmasked through local disinhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by bicuculline disinhibition experiments showing unmasking of twitch responses.

claim: Through P12, M1 sensory responses originate in the deep thalamorecipient layers, not primary somatosensory cortex.
source: Finally, through P12, M1 sensory responses originate in the deep thalamorecipient layers, not primary somatosensory cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by laminar recordings and cross-correlation analyses between M1 and S1.

claim: M1 initially establishes a sensory framework upon which its later-emerging role in motor control is built.
source: These findings demonstrate that M1 initially establishes a sensory framework upon which its later-emerging role in motor control is built.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the developmental sequence of sensory responses preceding motor functions.

claim: In rats, intracortical microstimulation of M1 neurons does not evoke movements until postnatal day (P) 35.
source: For example, in rats, intracortical microstimulation of M1 neurons does not evoke movements until postnatal day (P) 35 (Young et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Young et al., 2012.

claim: M1 neurons respond to externally generated (i.e. exafferent) stimulation beginning early in development in rats.
source: Beginning early in development in rats, M1 neurons respond to externally generated (i.e. exafferent) stimulation (An et al., 2014; Asanuma, 1981; Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to An et al., 2014; Asanuma, 1981; Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016.

claim: M1 neurons respond to sensory feedback (i.e. reafference) arising from myoclonic twitches.
source: In addition, M1 neurons respond to sensory feedback (i.e. reafference) arising from myoclonic twitches—the discrete, jerky movements produced abundantly and exclusively during active (REM) sleep (Tiriac et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tiriac et al., 2014.

claim: Myoclonic twitches are discrete, jerky movements produced abundantly and exclusively during active (REM) sleep.
source: In addition, M1 neurons respond to sensory feedback (i.e. reafference) arising from myoclonic twitches—the discrete, jerky movements produced abundantly and exclusively during active (REM) sleep (Tiriac et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a definitional claim about twitches supported by citation.

claim: Robust M1 responses to wake movement reafference are readily observed in adults.
source: With respect to reafference from wake movements, robust M1 responses are readily observed in adults (Asanuma, 1981; Fetz et al., 1980; Georgopoulos et al., 1982), but not in infants at 1 week of age (Tiriac et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Asanuma, 1981; Fetz et al., 1980; Georgopoulos et al., 1982.

claim: Wake-related reafference in the forelimb representation of M1 is suppressed in infants due to selective inhibition within the external cuneate nucleus (ECN).
source: Specifically, in infants, wake-related reafference in the forelimb representation of M1 is suppressed, due to selective inhibition within the external cuneate nucleus (ECN), a medullary nucleus that receives primary proprioceptive afferents from forelimb muscle spindles and conveys that afferent information to downstream structures (Boivie and Boman, 1981; Campbell et al., 1974); disinhibiting the infant ECN unmasks wake-related reafference (Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boivie and Boman, 1981; Campbell et al., 1974; Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016.

claim: The external cuneate nucleus (ECN) is a medullary nucleus that receives primary proprioceptive afferents from forelimb muscle spindles and conveys that afferent information to downstream structures.
source: Specifically, in infants, wake-related reafference in the forelimb representation of M1 is suppressed, due to selective inhibition within the external cuneate nucleus (ECN), a medullary nucleus that receives primary proprioceptive afferents from forelimb muscle spindles and conveys that afferent information to downstream structures (Boivie and Boman, 1981; Campbell et al., 1974); disinhibiting the infant ECN unmasks wake-related reafference (Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016).
evidence: This is an anatomical claim supported by citations to Boivie and Boman, 1981; Campbell et al., 1974.

claim: Disinhibiting the infant ECN unmasks wake-related reafference.
source: Specifically, in infants, wake-related reafference in the forelimb representation of M1 is suppressed, due to selective inhibition within the external cuneate nucleus (ECN), a medullary nucleus that receives primary proprioceptive afferents from forelimb muscle spindles and conveys that afferent information to downstream structures (Boivie and Boman, 1981; Campbell et al., 1974); disinhibiting the infant ECN unmasks wake-related reafference (Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016.

claim: In adults, proprioceptive input to M1 arrives both directly from thalamus and indirectly through primary somatosensory cortex (S1).
source: In adults, proprioceptive input to M1 arrives both directly from thalamus and indirectly through primary somatosensory cortex (S1; Asanuma, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Asanuma, 1981.

claim: Intracortical microstimulation of M1 neurons does not normally evoke movement until P35.
source: Interestingly, although intracortical microstimulation of M1 neurons does not normally evoke movement until P35, movements can be evoked at P13—but not at P12—after local disinhibition with the GABAA antagonist, bicuculline (Young et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Young et al., 2012.

claim: Movements can be evoked at P13—but not at P12—after local disinhibition with the GABAA antagonist, bicuculline.
source: Interestingly, although intracortical microstimulation of M1 neurons does not normally evoke movement until P35, movements can be evoked at P13—but not at P12—after local disinhibition with the GABAA antagonist, bicuculline (Young et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Young et al., 2012.

claim: As late as P12, corticospinal neurons are unable to directly drive movement.
source: This suggests that as late as P12, corticospinal neurons are unable to directly drive movement, which is consistent with the expansion of corticospinal axons in the spinal cord observed around this time (Curfs et al., 1994; Schreyer and Jones, 1982).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Curfs et al., 1994; Schreyer and Jones, 1982.

claim: Expansion of corticospinal axons in the spinal cord is observed around P12.
source: This suggests that as late as P12, corticospinal neurons are unable to directly drive movement, which is consistent with the expansion of corticospinal axons in the spinal cord observed around this time (Curfs et al., 1994; Schreyer and Jones, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Curfs et al., 1994; Schreyer and Jones, 1982.

claim: M1 neurons at P8-10 are exclusively responsive to reafference from twitches.
source: By performing extracellular recordings in the forelimb representation of M1 in unanesthetized P8-12 rats as they cycled between sleep and wake, we first show that M1 neurons at P8-10 are exclusively responsive to reafference from twitches, consistent with previous studies (Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016; Tiriac et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016; Tiriac et al., 2014.

claim: Between P10 and P12, M1 neurons suddenly begin to respond to reafference from wake movements.
source: Then, suddenly between P10 and P12, this pattern changes such that M1 neurons now respond to reafference from wake movements, but less often to twitches.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recordings showing the developmental transition.

claim: Between P10 and P12, M1 neurons respond less often to twitches.
source: Then, suddenly between P10 and P12, this pattern changes such that M1 neurons now respond to reafference from wake movements, but less often to twitches.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recordings showing decreased twitch responsiveness.

claim: M1 neurons at all ages respond to exafferent stimulation.
source: Because M1 neurons at all ages respond to exafferent stimulation, this developmental switch must be due specifically to changes in the processing of sensory input arising from self-generated movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing responses to exafferent stimulation across ages.

claim: The developmental switch in M1 responsiveness is due specifically to changes in the processing of sensory input arising from self-generated movements.
source: Because M1 neurons at all ages respond to exafferent stimulation, this developmental switch must be due specifically to changes in the processing of sensory input arising from self-generated movements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that exafferent responses remain constant while reafferent responses change.

claim: Around P12, there is an upstream change in the gating of wake-related reafference in the ECN.
source: To that end, we identify two separate developmental events around P12: (i) an upstream change in the gating of wake-related reafference in the ECN and (ii) a local suppression of twitch-related reafference within M1.
evidence: This claim is supported by ECN recordings showing changes in wake movement responsiveness.

claim: Around P12, there is a local suppression of twitch-related reafference within M1.
source: To that end, we identify two separate developmental events around P12: (i) an upstream change in the gating of wake-related reafference in the ECN and (ii) a local suppression of twitch-related reafference within M1.
evidence: This claim is supported by disinhibition experiments showing masked twitch responses.

claim: These developmental events comprise a rapid shift in M1 sensory processing that constitutes an 'awakening' to the sensory consequences of movement just before the developmental emergence of motor outflow.
source: Together, these events comprise a rapid shift in M1 sensory processing that constitutes an 'awakening' to the sensory consequences of movement just before the developmental emergence of motor outflow.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim summarizing the developmental findings.

claim: Neural activity was recorded from the forelimb representation of M1 in head-fixed, unanesthetized rats between P8 and P12.
source: We recorded neural activity from the forelimb representation of M1 in head-fixed, unanesthetized rats between P8 and P12 (P8: n = 10 pups, 160 neurons; P9: n = 9 pups, 112 neurons; P10: n = 8 pups, 123 neurons; P11: n = 15 pups, 197 neurons; P12 pups: n = 7, 165 neurons) using 4-shank silicon depth electrodes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,c; Table 1).
evidence: This is a methodological claim describing the experimental approach.

claim: Recordings were performed using 4-shank silicon depth electrodes.
source: We recorded neural activity from the forelimb representation of M1 in head-fixed, unanesthetized rats between P8 and P12 (P8: n = 10 pups, 160 neurons; P9: n = 9 pups, 112 neurons; P10: n = 8 pups, 123 neurons; P11: n = 15 pups, 197 neurons; P12 pups: n = 7, 165 neurons) using 4-shank silicon depth electrodes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,c; Table 1).
evidence: This is a methodological claim describing the recording technique.

claim: Electrode placement in the forelimb representation of M1 was confirmed through exafferent stimulation of the forelimb and subsequent staining of flattened, tangentially sectioned brains for cytochrome oxidase (CO).
source: We confirmed electrode placement in the forelimb representation of M1 through exafferent stimulation of the forelimb as well as subsequent staining of flattened, tangentially sectioned brains for cytochrome oxidase (CO; Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a methodological claim describing verification of recording location.

claim: M1 recording sites were restricted to agranular cortex immediately medial to S1.
source: M1 recording sites were restricted to agranular cortex immediately medial to S1 (Figure 1c–d).
evidence: This is a methodological claim describing the anatomical location of recordings.

claim: Recording depth was confirmed to be restricted to the deeper layers of cortex in a subset of coronally sectioned brains.
source: In a subset of coronally sectioned brains, recording depth was confirmed to be restricted to the deeper layers of cortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is a methodological claim describing verification of recording depth.

claim: At P8, M1 neurons exhibited more activity during periods of active sleep than during periods of wake.
source: As reported previously in P8 rats (Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016; Tiriac et al., 2014), neurons in the forelimb representation of M1 exhibited more activity during periods of active sleep than during periods of wake (Figure 1e, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016; Tiriac et al., 2014.

claim: Neuronal activity in M1 during active sleep clustered around forelimb twitches, but not wake movements at P8.
source: Perievent histograms revealed that neuronal activity in M1 during active sleep clustered around forelimb twitches, but not wake movements (Figure 1e, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by perievent histogram analysis of neural activity.

claim: The pattern of neural activity at P9 and P10 largely resembled that at P8.
source: The pattern of neural activity at P9 and P10 largely resembled that at P8.
evidence: This is a comparative claim based on experimental observations.

claim: At P11, M1 neurons were substantially more active during wake.
source: However, at P11, M1 neurons were substantially more active during wake (Figure 1f, left), with increased responsiveness to wake movements in addition to continued responsiveness to twitches (Figure 1f, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recordings at P11.

claim: At P11, M1 neurons showed increased responsiveness to wake movements in addition to continued responsiveness to twitches.
source: However, at P11, M1 neurons were substantially more active during wake (Figure 1f, left), with increased responsiveness to wake movements in addition to continued responsiveness to twitches (Figure 1f, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by perievent histogram analysis at P11.

claim: By P12, M1 neurons were continuously active during sleep and wake.
source: By P12, M1 neurons were continuously active during sleep and wake (Figure 1g, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recordings at P12.

claim: At P12, M1 activity increased after forelimb wake movements, but no longer increased after twitches.
source: Similar to P11, M1 activity increased after forelimb wake movements at P12, but no longer increased after twitches (Figure 1g, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by perievent histogram analysis at P12.

claim: Of the 757 M1 neurons recorded, not one showed a pattern of activity reflective of motor output—that is, an activity peak preceding movement.
source: Notably, of the 757 M1 neurons from which we recorded, not one showed a pattern of activity reflective of motor output—that is, an activity peak preceding movement (Del Rio-Bermudez et al., 2015)—thus providing the strongest evidence to date that M1 does not produce movement at these ages (see An et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of neural activity patterns with citation to Del Rio-Bermudez et al., 2015.

claim: M1 does not produce movement at P8-12.
source: Notably, of the 757 M1 neurons from which we recorded, not one showed a pattern of activity reflective of motor output—that is, an activity peak preceding movement (Del Rio-Bermudez et al., 2015)—thus providing the strongest evidence to date that M1 does not produce movement at these ages (see An et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of pre-movement activity patterns.

claim: Between P8 and P12, there was an age-related decrease in the number of forelimb twitches.
source: Between P8 and P12, we observed an age-related decrease in the number of forelimb twitches (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a, F(4,44) = 11.4, p<0.0001), consistent with previous reports (Marcano-Reik et al., 2010), but not in the number wake movements (F(4,44) = 1.1, p=0.37).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of movement counts with citation to Marcano-Reik et al., 2010.

claim: Between P8 and P12, there was no age-related change in the number of wake movements.
source: Between P8 and P12, we observed an age-related decrease in the number of forelimb twitches (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a, F(4,44) = 11.4, p<0.0001), consistent with previous reports (Marcano-Reik et al., 2010), but not in the number wake movements (F(4,44) = 1.1, p=0.37).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of movement counts.

claim: The EMG activity associated with twitches and wake movements did not change with age.
source: Importantly, because the EMG activity associated with twitches and wake movements did not change with age (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), any age-related changes in the reafferent responses of M1 neurons to twitches and wake movements cannot be attributed to changes in the duration of these movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by EMG analysis across ages.

claim: Age-related changes in the reafferent responses of M1 neurons to twitches and wake movements cannot be attributed to changes in the duration of these movements.
source: Importantly, because the EMG activity associated with twitches and wake movements did not change with age (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), any age-related changes in the reafferent responses of M1 neurons to twitches and wake movements cannot be attributed to changes in the duration of these movements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stability of EMG activity across ages.

claim: Twitches were fit to a symmetrical Gaussian function.
source: Twitches, being discrete movements, were fit to a symmetrical Gaussian function (Figure 2a) and wake movements were fit to an asymmetrical function comprising a Gaussian with an exponential decay (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a methodological claim describing the analysis approach.

claim: Wake movements were fit to an asymmetrical function comprising a Gaussian with an exponential decay.
source: Twitches, being discrete movements, were fit to a symmetrical Gaussian function (Figure 2a) and wake movements were fit to an asymmetrical function comprising a Gaussian with an exponential decay (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a methodological claim describing the analysis approach.

claim: A threshold r2 of 0.35 was selected to differentiate neurons that responded to twitches and wake movements from those that did not.
source: A threshold r2 of 0.35 was selected because it most effectively differentiated neurons that responded to twitches and wake movements from those that did not (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a methodological claim describing the classification criterion.

claim: There is a developmental shift in the neural population responses to twitches and wake movements, particularly between P10 and P12.
source: Scatterplots of r2twitch vs. r2wake for each neuron show a developmental shift in the neural population responses to twitches and wake movements, particularly between P10 and P12 (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by scatterplot analysis of neural responses.

claim: Most responsive neurons at P8 and P9 occupy the twitch-responsive quadrant.
source: Whereas most responsive neurons at P8 and P9 (and, to a lesser extent, P10) occupy the twitch-responsive quadrant (top-left, blue), by P11 most of the responsive neurons have shifted to the twitch- and wake-responsive quadrant (top-right, purple).
evidence: This claim is supported by scatterplot analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: By P11, most responsive neurons have shifted to the twitch- and wake-responsive quadrant.
source: Whereas most responsive neurons at P8 and P9 (and, to a lesser extent, P10) occupy the twitch-responsive quadrant (top-left, blue), by P11 most of the responsive neurons have shifted to the twitch- and wake-responsive quadrant (top-right, purple).
evidence: This claim is supported by scatterplot analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: By P12, most responsive neurons occupy the wake-responsive quadrant.
source: By P12 the population has shifted again, with most responsive neurons now occupying the wake-responsive quadrant (bottom-right, red).
evidence: This claim is supported by scatterplot analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Responsive neurons showed a significant decrease in r2twitch from P8 to P12, with the largest decrease between P11 and P12.
source: This population-level shift in responsivity is supported quantitatively, with responsive neurons showing a significant decrease in r2twitch from P8 to P12, the largest decrease being between P11 and P12 (Figure 3b, blue bars; H(4,321) = 85.4, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of r2 values.

claim: r2wake increased from P8 to P12.
source: Correspondingly, r2wake increased from P8 to P12 (Figure 3b, red bars; H(4,321) = 119.6, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of r2 values.

claim: All responsive neurons also responded to exafferent stimulation of the forelimb.
source: Importantly, all responsive neurons also responded to exafferent stimulation of the forelimb (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a; green lines), thus demonstrating consistency in the recorded neuron's receptive field across age.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing responses to exafferent stimulation.

claim: The strongest M1 neural responses at P8 and P12 were found in layers 5b and 6.
source: At both ages, the strongest M1 neural responses were found in layers 5b and 6 (Figure 4b,d; upper).
evidence: This claim is supported by laminar electrode recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: Current source density analysis revealed a current sink in layers 5a and 5b at P8 and P12.
source: Consistent with this, current source density analysis revealed a current sink in layers 5a and 5b (Figure 4b,d; lower).
evidence: This claim is supported by current source density analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Sensory input to M1 arrives directly from the thalamus.
source: From these observations, we conclude that sensory input to M1 arrives directly from the thalamus.
evidence: This is an inference based on laminar recordings and current source density analysis.

claim: Anatomical evidence suggests that horizontal projections between S1 and M1 do not drive neural activity in the deeper layers before P12.
source: Although anatomical evidence suggests that horizontal projections between S1 and M1 do not drive neural activity in the deeper layers before P12 (Anastasiades and Butt, 2012), we nonetheless assessed whether M1 reafference is conveyed via S1 by recording simultaneously from M1 and S1 at P8 (n = 6 pups, 94 M1 neurons, 91 S1 neurons) and P12 (n = 6 pups, 135 M1 neurons, 107 S1 neurons; Figure 5a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anastasiades and Butt, 2012.

claim: At P8 and P12, there are striking similarities between the activity profiles of responsive neurons in S1 and M1 to the same movements.
source: At both ages, we observed striking similarities between the activity profiles of responsive neurons in S1 and M1 to the same movements (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by simultaneous recordings from M1 and S1 shown in Figure 5.

claim: Event-triggered S1 activity was typically contemporaneous with M1 activity.
source: This analysis revealed that event-triggered S1 activity was typically contemporaneous with M1 activity (Figure 5c,d), thus ruling out the conveyance of reafference from S1 to M1 via horizontal projections.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The contemporaneous activity of S1 and M1 rules out the conveyance of reafference from S1 to M1 via horizontal projections.
source: This analysis revealed that event-triggered S1 activity was typically contemporaneous with M1 activity (Figure 5c,d), thus ruling out the conveyance of reafference from S1 to M1 via horizontal projections.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of S1 and M1 activity.

claim: At P8-10, the ECN acts as a sensory gate that selectively blocks wake-related reafference.
source: At P8-10, the ECN acts as a sensory gate that selectively blocks wake-related reafference (Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016; Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016 and illustrated in Figure 6a.

claim: The sudden emergence of wake movement responses at P11-12 reflects the opening of the ECN's sensory gate.
source: Thus, we hypothesized that the sudden emergence of wake movement responses at P11-12 reflects the opening of the ECN's sensory gate (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by ECN recordings.

claim: At P9, ECN neurons show robust responses to forelimb twitches, but not wake movements.
source: As described previously (Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016), we observed robust responses in P9 ECN neurons to forelimb twitches, but not wake movements (Figure 6c).
evidence: This claim is supported by ECN recordings at P9 with citation to Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016.

claim: At P12, ECN neurons responded to both twitches and wake movements.
source: At P12, however, ECN neurons responded to both twitches and wake movements (Figure 6d).
evidence: This claim is supported by ECN recordings at P12 shown in Figure 6d.

claim: At P12, ECN activity reliably preceded M1 activity by 15 ms.
source: Further, at P12, we again analyzed the data using the shift predictor and found that ECN activity reliably preceded M1 activity by 15 ms (Figure 6—figure supplement 1f), consistent with ECN inputs projecting to the forelimb representation of M1.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1f.

claim: ECN neurons at P9 were predominantly responsive to twitches (11 of 16 neurons).
source: Whereas ECN neurons at P9 were predominantly responsive to twitches (Figure 7a, left; 11 of 16 neurons), ECN neurons at P12 were responsive to both twitches and wake movements (Figure 7a, right; 15 of 20 neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by classification of ECN neurons shown in Figure 7a.

claim: ECN neurons at P12 were responsive to both twitches and wake movements (15 of 20 neurons).
source: Whereas ECN neurons at P9 were predominantly responsive to twitches (Figure 7a, left; 11 of 16 neurons), ECN neurons at P12 were responsive to both twitches and wake movements (Figure 7a, right; 15 of 20 neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by classification of ECN neurons shown in Figure 7a.

claim: P9 and P12 ECN neurons were similarly twitch-responsive.
source: Consequently, although P9 and P12 ECN neurons were similarly twitch-responsive (Figure 7b, blue bars; t34 = 1.8, p=0.09), P12 neurons were significantly more wake-responsive than P9 neurons (Figure 7b, red bars; t34 = 2.9, p=0.006), resulting in very different distributions at these ages (Figure 7c).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of ECN neuron responses shown in Figure 7b.

claim: P12 ECN neurons were significantly more wake-responsive than P9 neurons.
source: Consequently, although P9 and P12 ECN neurons were similarly twitch-responsive (Figure 7b, blue bars; t34 = 1.8, p=0.09), P12 neurons were significantly more wake-responsive than P9 neurons (Figure 7b, red bars; t34 = 2.9, p=0.006), resulting in very different distributions at these ages (Figure 7c).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of ECN neuron responses shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The increase in wake responsiveness of M1 neurons at P11 and P12 is due to a state-dependent change in sensory gating in the ECN.
source: Based on these findings, we conclude that the increase in wake responsiveness of M1 neurons at P11 and P12 is due to a state-dependent change in sensory gating in the ECN.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on ECN recordings showing developmental changes in wake responsiveness.

claim: At P12, neurons in the ECN continue to respond to twitch-related reafference.
source: At P12, neurons in the ECN continue to respond to twitch-related reafference; accordingly, the decrease in twitch-related activity in M1 neurons cannot be attributed to the ECN.
evidence: This claim is supported by ECN recordings at P12 showing continued twitch responsiveness.

claim: The decrease in twitch-related activity in M1 neurons at P12 cannot be attributed to the ECN.
source: At P12, neurons in the ECN continue to respond to twitch-related reafference; accordingly, the decrease in twitch-related activity in M1 neurons cannot be attributed to the ECN.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ECN neurons remain twitch-responsive at P12.

claim: Twitch-related reafference continues to reach M1 at P12, but changes in local circuitry serve to mask this activity.
source: One possibility is that twitch-related reafference continues to reach M1 at P12, but changes in local circuitry—particularly local inhibitory circuitry—serve to mask this activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by disinhibition experiments.

claim: Local disinhibition of M1 should unmask responses to twitches if twitch-related reafference continues to reach M1 at P12.
source: If true, local disinhibition of M1 should unmask responses to twitches.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis about local inhibition.

claim: Drug diffusion was largely confined to the forelimb representation of M1 in bicuculline experiments.
source: Also, by adding Fluoro-Gold to the solution and using its spread as a proxy for the spread of bicuculline, we confirmed that drug diffusion was largely confined to the forelimb representation of M1 (Figure 8a,b).
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by histological verification shown in Figure 8.

claim: Before injection of bicuculline, M1 neurons were predominantly wake-responsive.
source: Likewise, before the injection of bicuculline, M1 neurons were predominantly wake-responsive (Figure 8c, bottom left).
evidence: This claim is supported by pre-injection recordings shown in Figure 8c.

claim: After injection of bicuculline, there was a clear increase in twitch-responsiveness of the previously wake-responsive neurons.
source: However, after injection of bicuculline, there was a clear increase in twitch-responsiveness of the previously wake-responsive neurons (Figure 8c, bottom right).
evidence: This claim is supported by post-injection recordings shown in Figure 8c.

claim: M1 neurons exhibited increased r2twitch values after injection of bicuculline.
source: Quantitatively, as shown in Figure 8d, M1 neurons exhibited increased r2twitch values after injection of bicuculline (Z65 = 6.8, p<0.0001), with no corresponding change in r2wake (Z65 = 1.8, p=0.08); saline injection had no effect on either r2twitch or r2wake.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of r2 values shown in Figure 8d.

claim: Saline injection had no effect on either r2twitch or r2wake.
source: Quantitatively, as shown in Figure 8d, M1 neurons exhibited increased r2twitch values after injection of bicuculline (Z65 = 6.8, p<0.0001), with no corresponding change in r2wake (Z65 = 1.8, p=0.08); saline injection had no effect on either r2twitch or r2wake.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of control experiments shown in Figure 8d.

claim: Local disinhibition of M1 neurons unmasked twitch-related reafference.
source: Because local disinhibition of M1 neurons unmasked twitch-related reafference (Figure 8e), it is clear that twitch-related reafference reaches M1 at P12, just as it does at P8.
evidence: This claim is supported by bicuculline experiments shown in Figure 8e.

claim: Twitch-related reafference reaches M1 at P12, just as it does at P8.
source: Because local disinhibition of M1 neurons unmasked twitch-related reafference (Figure 8e), it is clear that twitch-related reafference reaches M1 at P12, just as it does at P8.
evidence: This is an inference based on the unmasking of twitch responses by disinhibition.

claim: M1 neurons at P8 were overwhelmingly responsive to twitch-related reafference.
source: Consistent with previous reports, we found that M1 neurons at P8 were overwhelmingly responsive to twitch-related reafference; in contrast, reafference from wake movements failed to trigger M1 activity due to sensory gating at the ECN (Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016.

claim: Reafference from wake movements failed to trigger M1 activity at P8 due to sensory gating at the ECN.
source: Consistent with previous reports, we found that M1 neurons at P8 were overwhelmingly responsive to twitch-related reafference; in contrast, reafference from wake movements failed to trigger M1 activity due to sensory gating at the ECN (Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016.

claim: The pattern of M1 responsiveness persisted through P10.
source: This pattern persisted through P10.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recordings at P8-10.

claim: At P11, M1 neurons suddenly exhibited robust responses to wake-related reafference.
source: Then, at P11, M1 neurons suddenly exhibited robust responses to wake-related reafference, a developmental 'awakening' that, as demonstrated here, results from an upstream change in state-dependent sensory processing of self-generated movements in the ECN.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recordings at P11.

claim: The developmental 'awakening' at P11 results from an upstream change in state-dependent sensory processing of self-generated movements in the ECN.
source: Then, at P11, M1 neurons suddenly exhibited robust responses to wake-related reafference, a developmental 'awakening' that, as demonstrated here, results from an upstream change in state-dependent sensory processing of self-generated movements in the ECN.
evidence: This claim is supported by ECN recordings showing developmental changes.

claim: By P12, twitch-related reafference continues to reach M1 neurons, but is less likely to drive neural activity.
source: By P12, twitch-related reafference continues to reach M1 neurons, but is less likely to drive neural activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by recordings and disinhibition experiments at P12.

claim: M1 sensory responses originate in the deep layers of M1 and occur nearly simultaneously with sensory responses in S1.
source: Further, we demonstrated that these M1 sensory responses originate in the deep layers of M1, and occur nearly simultaneously with sensory responses in S1, suggesting parallel thalamic inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by laminar recordings and cross-correlation analysis.

claim: The nearly simultaneous sensory responses in M1 and S1 suggest parallel thalamic inputs.
source: Further, we demonstrated that these M1 sensory responses originate in the deep layers of M1, and occur nearly simultaneously with sensory responses in S1, suggesting parallel thalamic inputs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of M1 and S1 responses.

claim: M1 is built on a sensory framework that scaffolds its later-emerging motor map.
source: The present findings strongly support the idea that M1 is built on a sensory framework that scaffolds its later-emerging motor map (Chakrabarty and Martin, 2005; Huntley, 1997b; Keller et al., 1996).
evidence: This is an interpretive claim supported by the developmental findings and citations to Chakrabarty and Martin, 2005; Huntley, 1997b; Keller et al., 1996.

claim: M1's sensory framework lays a foundation for plasticity in adulthood.
source: Further, our findings suggest that M1's sensory framework lays a foundation for this plasticity in adulthood.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the functional significance of the sensory framework.

claim: Twitches provide a robust source of proprioceptive input to M1 neurons for early sensorimotor development.
source: Similar to spontaneous retinal waves for the developing visual system (Ackman et al., 2012; Hanganu et al., 2006) and spontaneous cochlear activity for the developing auditory system (Tritsch et al., 2007), twitches provide a robust source of proprioceptive input to M1 neurons for early sensorimotor development (Blumberg, 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ackman et al., 2012; Hanganu et al., 2006; Tritsch et al., 2007; Blumberg, 2015b.

claim: Twitches are low-amplitude, discrete events that occur against a background of low muscle tone.
source: First, unlike wake movements, twitches are low-amplitude, discrete events that occur against a background of low muscle tone; these features enable individual twitches to provide high-fidelity reafferent signals to the developing brain.
evidence: This is a descriptive claim about the characteristics of twitches.

claim: Individual twitches provide high-fidelity reafferent signals to the developing brain.
source: First, unlike wake movements, twitches are low-amplitude, discrete events that occur against a background of low muscle tone; these features enable individual twitches to provide high-fidelity reafferent signals to the developing brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of twitches.

claim: Twitches occur exclusively and abundantly during active sleep, the predominant behavioral state in early development.
source: Second, twitches occur exclusively and abundantly during active sleep, the predominant behavioral state in early development (Jouvet-Mounier et al., 1970; Kayser and Biron, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jouvet-Mounier et al., 1970; Kayser and Biron, 2016.

claim: Active sleep is the predominant behavioral state in early development.
source: Second, twitches occur exclusively and abundantly during active sleep, the predominant behavioral state in early development (Jouvet-Mounier et al., 1970; Kayser and Biron, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jouvet-Mounier et al., 1970; Kayser and Biron, 2016.

claim: Sensory feedback from twitches is the only reliable source of self-generated proprioceptive input to M1 neurons before P10.
source: Finally, when combined with the inhibition of wake-related reafference in ECN neurons (Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016), which prevents this reafference from being conveyed to neurons in M1, sensory feedback from twitches is the only reliable source of self-generated proprioceptive input to M1 neurons before P10.
evidence: This is an inference based on the selective gating of wake-related reafference with citation to Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016.

claim: Twitches are self-generated movements that typically occur in rapid succession in nearby muscles.
source: Twitches are self-generated movements that typically occur in rapid succession in nearby muscles (Blumberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blumberg et al., 2013.

claim: At P8-10, all responsive neurons were twitch-responsive and twitches of just one muscle triggered responses in half of the M1 neurons recorded.
source: At P8-10, all responsive neurons were twitch-responsive and the twitches of just one muscle—the bicep—triggered responses in half of the M1 neurons from which we recorded (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b); this suggests that each M1 neuron's receptive field encompassed multiple forelimb muscles.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of neuron classifications shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Each M1 neuron's receptive field at P8-10 encompassed multiple forelimb muscles.
source: At P8-10, all responsive neurons were twitch-responsive and the twitches of just one muscle—the bicep—triggered responses in half of the M1 neurons from which we recorded (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b); this suggests that each M1 neuron's receptive field encompassed multiple forelimb muscles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proportion of neurons responding to bicep twitches.

claim: Neurons that were unresponsive to twitches and wake movements were nonetheless responsive to exafferent forelimb stimulation.
source: Also, it should be noted that those neurons that were unresponsive to twitches and wake movements were nonetheless responsive to exafferent forelimb stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a), almost certainly because the method of exafferent stimulation entails stimulation of receptors throughout the limb.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The percentage of twitch-responsive neurons in M1 decreased suddenly by P12.
source: The percentage of twitch-responsive neurons in M1 decreased suddenly by P12 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: At P11, 73% of responsive M1 neurons were twitch-responsive.
source: At P11, of the responsive M1 neurons, 73% were twitch-responsive; by P12, that percentage had decreased to just 24% (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: By P12, only 24% of responsive M1 neurons were twitch-responsive.
source: At P11, of the responsive M1 neurons, 73% were twitch-responsive; by P12, that percentage had decreased to just 24% (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The sudden decrease in twitch responsiveness at P12 is attributable to local inhibition.
source: This sudden decrease in twitch responsiveness is attributable to local inhibition, as disinhibiting M1 using the GABAA antagonist, bicuculline, restored twitch responsiveness to 71% (Figure 8c–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by bicuculline experiments shown in Figure 8c-e.

claim: Disinhibiting M1 using bicuculline restored twitch responsiveness to 71%.
source: This sudden decrease in twitch responsiveness is attributable to local inhibition, as disinhibiting M1 using the GABAA antagonist, bicuculline, restored twitch responsiveness to 71% (Figure 8c–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by bicuculline experiments shown in Figure 8c-e.

claim: There is a rapid change in the excitatory-inhibitory balance in M1 between P11 and P12.
source: That M1 neurons remained twitch-responsive just 1 day earlier suggests a rapid change in the excitatory-inhibitory balance in M1 between P11 and P12, which could be due to changes in interneuron network connectivity as well as changes in the postsynaptic effects of GABA (Ben-Ari et al., 2007; Blaesse et al., 2009; Payne et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid developmental change with citations to Ben-Ari et al., 2007; Blaesse et al., 2009; Payne et al., 2003.

claim: By P12, some sensory inputs to M1 neurons persist beneath a layer of inhibitory control.
source: Thus, by P12 some sensory inputs to M1 neurons persist beneath a layer of inhibitory control.
evidence: This is an inference based on the unmasking of twitch responses by disinhibition.

claim: Similar subthreshold inputs in M1 have been demonstrated previously in adults.
source: Similar subthreshold inputs in M1 have been demonstrated previously in adults, and it has been suggested that they constitute the latent connections that permit rapid M1 plasticity (Huntley, 1997a; Jacobs and Donoghue, 1991; Peters et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huntley, 1997a; Jacobs and Donoghue, 1991; Peters et al., 2017.

claim: Subthreshold inputs constitute the latent connections that permit rapid M1 plasticity.
source: Similar subthreshold inputs in M1 have been demonstrated previously in adults, and it has been suggested that they constitute the latent connections that permit rapid M1 plasticity (Huntley, 1997a; Jacobs and Donoghue, 1991; Peters et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huntley, 1997a; Jacobs and Donoghue, 1991; Peters et al., 2017.

claim: The broad receptive fields of M1 neurons at P8-10 reveal the foundation of M1's sensory framework and the maximal extent of rapid adult plasticity in that structure.
source: Accordingly, we propose that the broad receptive fields of M1 neurons at P8-10 reveal the foundation of M1's sensory framework and the maximal extent of rapid adult plasticity in that structure.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the functional significance of broad receptive fields.

claim: Twitch responses at P8 and P12 suggest a sharpening of the M1 receptive fields with age.
source: Closer inspection of twitch responses at P8 and P12 suggests a sharpening of the M1 receptive fields with age, such that a smaller subset of neurons become more consistently driven by the movement of individual muscles (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sharpening of receptive fields such that neurons are responsive only to preferred stimuli has been termed the 'iceberg effect'.
source: In the context of inhibition, this type of sharpening—such that neurons are responsive only to preferred stimuli—has been termed the 'iceberg effect' (Carandini and Ferster, 2000; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Rose and Blakemore, 1974) and has been demonstrated across several sensory modalities (Liu et al., 2011; Poo and Isaacson, 2009; Wu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carandini and Ferster, 2000; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Rose and Blakemore, 1974; Liu et al., 2011; Poo and Isaacson, 2009; Wu et al., 2008.

claim: The robust sensory response of M1 neurons to twitches at P8-10 stands in sharp contrast to their conspicuous silence following wake movements.
source: The robust sensory response of M1 neurons to twitches at P8-10 stands in sharp contrast to their conspicuous silence following wake movements (Figure 1e, see Tiriac et al., 2014)—a silence highlighted further by the sudden influx of wake-movement reafference at P11 (Figure 1e,f; Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e with citation to Tiriac et al., 2014.

claim: The transition in wake responsiveness at P11 is the result of a rapid change in the processing of wake-related reafference in the ECN.
source: This transition—the result of a rapid change in the processing of wake-related reafference in the ECN—represents a milestone in the development of the sensorimotor system.
evidence: This claim is supported by ECN recordings showing developmental changes.

claim: The transition in wake responsiveness at P11 represents a milestone in the development of the sensorimotor system.
source: This transition—the result of a rapid change in the processing of wake-related reafference in the ECN—represents a milestone in the development of the sensorimotor system.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim about the developmental significance of the transition.

claim: Neurons in the developing visual cortex are initially blind to patterned light.
source: Just as neurons in the developing visual cortex are initially blind to patterned light (Colonnese et al., 2010)—instead relying on retinal waves for early retinotopic development—neurons in M1 are initially 'blind' to the consequences of wake movements, relying instead on sensory feedback provided by twitches.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Colonnese et al., 2010.

claim: Neurons in M1 are initially 'blind' to the consequences of wake movements, relying instead on sensory feedback provided by twitches.
source: Just as neurons in the developing visual cortex are initially blind to patterned light (Colonnese et al., 2010)—instead relying on retinal waves for early retinotopic development—neurons in M1 are initially 'blind' to the consequences of wake movements, relying instead on sensory feedback provided by twitches.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim drawing an analogy to visual system development.

claim: Retinal waves drive cortical activity across periods of sleep and wake.
source: Interestingly, although retinal waves drive cortical activity across periods of sleep and wake (Ackman et al., 2012), analogous neural activity in the developing sensorimotor system occurs exclusively during active sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ackman et al., 2012.

claim: Analogous neural activity in the developing sensorimotor system occurs exclusively during active sleep.
source: Interestingly, although retinal waves drive cortical activity across periods of sleep and wake (Ackman et al., 2012), analogous neural activity in the developing sensorimotor system occurs exclusively during active sleep.
evidence: This is a comparative claim based on the state-dependence of twitch-related activity.

claim: Even the weakest visual input can generate a saturating response in developing visual cortex.
source: Here again, we can draw upon work in the developing visual system showing that even the weakest visual input can generate a saturating response in cortex (Colonnese et al., 2010; for review see Colonnese and Phillips, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Colonnese et al., 2010; Colonnese and Phillips, 2018.

claim: If similar cortical circuitry in the developing sensorimotor system permitted twitches to generate a saturating response in M1 and S1, wake movements would likely result in sustained, global activation.
source: If similar cortical circuitry in the developing sensorimotor system permitted twitches to generate a saturating response in M1 and S1, wake movements—if conveyed to M1—would likely result in sustained, global activation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential consequences of wake movement reafference.

claim: Reafference from wake movements could weaken somatotopic boundaries across sensorimotor cortex during this sensitive period of development.
source: As wake movements are not temporally restricted to individual body parts, reafference from wake movements could weaken somatotopic boundaries across sensorimotor cortex during this sensitive period of development.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential developmental consequences.

claim: For M1 neurons to contribute to motor learning, they must eventually be sensitive to feedback from wake movements.
source: Regardless, for M1 neurons to contribute to motor learning, they must eventually be sensitive to feedback from wake movements.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for motor learning.

claim: The critical transition in the responsiveness of both M1 and ECN neurons to wake movements occurs suddenly between P10 and P12.
source: As demonstrated here, the critical transition in the responsiveness of both M1 and ECN neurons to wake movements occurs suddenly between P10 and P12.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recordings from M1 and ECN.

claim: The transition in wake responsiveness enables wake movements to differentially activate populations of M1 neurons.
source: This transition enables wake movements to differentially activate populations of M1 neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the emergence of wake responsiveness.

claim: Early differential patterns of activation are precursors to the activity of 'movement-related neurons' in adult M1.
source: These early differential patterns of activation are precursors to the activity of 'movement-related neurons' in adult M1, as described by others (Hyland, 1998; Komiyama et al., 2010; Peters et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative claim with citations to Hyland, 1998; Komiyama et al., 2010; Peters et al., 2014.

claim: The increase in wake responsiveness of M1 neurons at P12 provides an essential bridge linking their sensory activity during the first postnatal week with their sensory activity after M1 has established its motor functions.
source: Thus, the increase in wake responsiveness of M1 neurons at P12 provides an essential bridge linking their sensory activity during the first postnatal week (Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016; Tiriac et al., 2014) with their sensory activity after M1 has established its motor functions.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim about the developmental significance with citations to Tiriac and Blumberg, 2016; Tiriac et al., 2014.

claim: In adults, the functional importance of wake-movement reafference for M1 motor control is well established.
source: In adults, the functional importance of wake-movement reafference for M1 motor control is well established (Iriki et al., 1989; Iriki et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Iriki et al., 1989; Iriki et al., 1991.

claim: At P12, M1 neurons are not yet involved in motor control.
source: However, at P12, M1 neurons are not yet involved in motor control.
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of motor-related activity patterns.

claim: Early wake-movement reafference shapes emerging motor control and plasticity.
source: We propose that early wake-movement reafference shapes emerging motor control and plasticity.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the function of early wake-movement reafference.

claim: In adults, plasticity in M1 is driven through the coincident activation of both horizontal projections from S1 and ascending projections from thalamus.
source: Although adult M1 neurons receive a diversity of cortical and thalamic inputs, plasticity is driven through the coincident activation of both horizontal projections from S1 and ascending projections from thalamus (Iriki et al., 1989; Iriki et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Iriki et al., 1989; Iriki et al., 1991.

claim: At P12, horizontal projections to M1 neurons are present, but the synaptic connections from superficial to deeper layers are silent.
source: At P12, horizontal projections to M1 neurons are present, but the synaptic connections from superficial to deeper layers are silent; because of these 'silent synapses,' S1 input to M1 is incapable of driving corticospinal neurons (Anastasiades and Butt, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anastasiades and Butt, 2012.

claim: Because of 'silent synapses,' S1 input to M1 is incapable of driving corticospinal neurons at P12.
source: At P12, horizontal projections to M1 neurons are present, but the synaptic connections from superficial to deeper layers are silent; because of these 'silent synapses,' S1 input to M1 is incapable of driving corticospinal neurons (Anastasiades and Butt, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anastasiades and Butt, 2012.

claim: Wake-movement reafference drives activity in deep M1 neurons via ascending (i.e. thalamic) projections at P12.
source: However, as demonstrated here, wake-movement reafference drives activity in deep M1 neurons via ascending (i.e. thalamic) projections.
evidence: This claim is supported by laminar recordings and current source density analysis.

claim: The ascending source of reafference may contribute to the functional conversion of the previously silent synapses.
source: Accordingly, the ascending source of reafference described here may contribute to the functional conversion of the previously silent synapses.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the role of ascending reafference.

claim: The corticospinal tract is sufficiently developed to produce M1-mediated movements as early as P13.
source: Intracortical microstimulation experiments in rats reveal that the corticospinal tract is sufficiently developed to produce M1-mediated movements as early as P13, although inhibition on corticospinal neurons appears to limit motor outflow for several additional weeks (Young et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Young et al., 2012.

claim: Inhibition on corticospinal neurons appears to limit motor outflow for several additional weeks after P13.
source: Intracortical microstimulation experiments in rats reveal that the corticospinal tract is sufficiently developed to produce M1-mediated movements as early as P13, although inhibition on corticospinal neurons appears to limit motor outflow for several additional weeks (Young et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Young et al., 2012.

claim: For motor outflow to occur, inhibition of M1 corticospinal neurons must be overcome by sufficiently strong excitation.
source: Thus, for motor outflow to occur, inhibition of M1 corticospinal neurons must be overcome by sufficiently strong excitation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the balance of excitation and inhibition.

claim: Repeated reafference arising from subcortically generated wake movements provides synapses on deep M1 neurons the opportunity to be shaped and strengthened.
source: We suggest that repeated reafference arising from subcortically generated wake movements provides synapses on deep M1 neurons the opportunity to be shaped and strengthened, producing increased excitatory drive onto corticospinal neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the role of repeated reafference.

claim: With sufficient repetition, excitatory drive can allow M1 motor neurons to contribute to movement.
source: With sufficient repetition, this excitatory drive can allow M1 motor neurons to contribute to movement.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the developmental outcome.

claim: The traditional designation of primary motor and sensory cortices as exclusively 'motor' and 'sensory,' respectively, is contradicted by neurophysiological and comparative studies.
source: The traditional designation of primary motor and sensory cortices as exclusively 'motor' and 'sensory,' respectively, is contradicted by neurophysiological and comparative studies (Asanuma, 1981; Baldwin et al., 2017; Baldwin et al., 2018; Cooke et al., 2015; Hatsopoulos and Suminski, 2011; Lende, 1963a; Matyas et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Asanuma, 1981; Baldwin et al., 2017; Baldwin et al., 2018; Cooke et al., 2015; Hatsopoulos and Suminski, 2011; Lende, 1963a; Matyas et al., 2010.

claim: Placental mammals have an M1, but many marsupials do not.
source: From a comparative perspective, placental mammals have an M1, but many marsupials do not (Kaas, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kaas, 2004.

claim: Virginia opossums have what has been referred to as a 'sensorimotor amalgam' that exhibits a mix of features of S1 and M1 as defined in placental mammals.
source: For example, Virginia opossums have what has been referred to as a 'sensorimotor amalgam' that exhibits a mix of features of S1 and M1 as defined in placental mammals (Karlen and Krubitzer, 2007; Lende, 1963a; Lende, 1963b; Lende, 1963c).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Karlen and Krubitzer, 2007; Lende, 1963a; Lende, 1963b; Lende, 1963c.

claim: S1 and M1 are derived from the same ancestral brain area and opossums have retained this ancestral state.
source: This has led to the hypothesis that S1 and M1 are derived from the same ancestral brain area and that opossums have retained this ancestral state (Beck et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation to Beck et al., 1996.

claim: M1's shared evolutionary history with somatosensory cortex suggests that it should develop similarly to other somatosensory areas, including S1.
source: Even though M1 in rats is highly specialized, its shared evolutionary history with somatosensory cortex suggests that it should develop similarly to other somatosensory areas, including S1.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary considerations.

claim: Evolution enables phenotypic transformations in cortical structure through alterations in developmental processes.
source: This suggestion is consistent with a developmental-evolutionary perspective, according to which evolution enables phenotypic transformations in cortical structure through alterations in developmental processes (Krubitzer and Dooley, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krubitzer and Dooley, 2013.

claim: Earlier in development, M1 and S1 should exhibit more shared features.
source: Thus, earlier in development, M1 and S1 should exhibit more shared features.
evidence: This is an inference based on the developmental-evolutionary perspective.

claim: M1 and S1 exhibit similar sensory response profiles.
source: This idea gains support here from the similar sensory response profiles observed in M1 and S1 and the evidence that both sensory input to both structures arises from parallel ascending pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by simultaneous recordings from M1 and S1.

claim: Sensory input to both M1 and S1 arises from parallel ascending pathways.
source: This idea gains support here from the similar sensory response profiles observed in M1 and S1 and the evidence that both sensory input to both structures arises from parallel ascending pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by laminar recordings and cross-correlation analysis.

claim: M1's sensory framework lays a foundation for plasticity in adulthood.
source: Unique to the present investigation, we have identified the relative contributions of sensory feedback from self-generated sleep and wake movements to M1's somatotopically organized activity. Unlike the developing visual system, behavioral state provides a critical context for characterizing the sensory development of M1 neurons. Further, our findings suggest that M1's sensory framework lays a foundation for this plasticity in adulthood.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the functional significance of the sensory framework.

claim: Therapeutic outcomes for stroke patients would improve if closer attention were paid to also assessing and restoring proprioceptive function.
source: Alternatively, it has been suggested that therapeutic outcomes for stroke patients would improve if closer attention were paid to also assessing and restoring proprioceptive function (Semrau et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Semrau et al., 2015.

claim: Understanding the mechanisms of normal development can help inform therapies that promote recovery following stroke.
source: Moreover, if understanding the mechanisms of normal development can help inform therapies that promote recovery following stroke (Johnston, 2009; Murphy and Corbett, 2009), then the present results suggest that the degree of early sensory recovery will predict eventual motor recovery and inform therapeutic interventions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Johnston, 2009; Murphy and Corbett, 2009.

claim: The degree of early sensory recovery will predict eventual motor recovery and inform therapeutic interventions.
source: Moreover, if understanding the mechanisms of normal development can help inform therapies that promote recovery following stroke (Johnston, 2009; Murphy and Corbett, 2009), then the present results suggest that the degree of early sensory recovery will predict eventual motor recovery and inform therapeutic interventions.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about clinical implications.

claim: In juvenile and adult mice, active sleep appears to critically influence the elimination and stabilization of new dendritic spines in M1 formed in a motor learning task.
source: For example, in juvenile and adult mice, active sleep appears to critically influence the elimination and stabilization of new dendritic spines in M1 formed in a motor learning task (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2017.

claim: In finches, consolidation of song motor memories depends on neural processes during active sleep.
source: For example, in finches, consolidation of song motor memories also depends on neural processes during active sleep (Brawn et al., 2010; Derégnaucourt et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brawn et al., 2010; Derégnaucourt et al., 2005.

claim: The present findings encourage a new conceptualization of how M1 is functionally organized and how it adapts to and supports learning across the lifespan.
source: Thus, all together, the present findings encourage a new conceptualization of how M1 is functionally organized and how it adapts to and supports learning across the lifespan.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim about the broader implications of the findings.
